question.prompt: The least common multiple of \(a\) and \(b\) is \(12,\) and the least common multiple of \(b\) and \(c\) is \(15.\) What is the least possible value of the least common multiple of \(a\) and \(c?\)

solutions.explanation:
A least common multiple is a multiple of each input, so \(b\) must divide both \(12\) and \(15\). Their only common positive divisors are \(1\) and \(3\), so \(b\) is one of these two numbers.

Also, \(a\) must divide \(12\), whose divisors are \(1,2,3,4,6,12\). Pairing any of \(1,2,3,6\) with either possible value of \(b\) gives a least common multiple at most \(6\). Thus \(a\) must be \(4\) or \(12\), so it is a multiple of \(4\).

Similarly, \(c\) divides \(15\), so it is \(1,3,5\), or \(15\). Neither \(1\) nor \(3\), paired with \(b\), can give a least common multiple of \(15\). Therefore \(c\) is \(5\) or \(15\), so it is a multiple of \(5\).

Consequently, every common multiple of \(a\) and \(c\) must be a multiple of both \(4\) and \(5\). The least such positive number is \(20\). To show that this lower bound can actually occur, choose
\[
(a,b,c)=(4,3,5).
\]
Then \(\operatorname{lcm}(4,3)=12\), \(\operatorname{lcm}(3,5)=15\), and \(\operatorname{lcm}(4,5)=20\). The least possible value is therefore \(\boxed{20}\), choice \(\text{A}\).
